orig_sentences: As a modern author writes, “it is not essential to be a dupe.”
The attitudes of which I shall treat can assume their whole meaning only through consideration of their contraries.
A sub-clerk in the post office is the equal of a conqueror if consciousness is common to them.
All experiences are indifferent in this regard.
There are some that do either a service or a disservice to man.
They do him a service if he is conscious.
Otherwise, that has no importance: a man’s failures imply judgment, not of circumstances, but of himself.
I am choosing solely men who aim only to expend themselves or whom I see to be expending themselves.
That has no further implications.
For the moment I want to speak only of a world in which thoughts, like lives, are devoid of future.
Everything that makes man work and get excited utilizes hope.
The sole thought that is not mendacious is therefore a sterile thought.
In the absurd world the value of a notion or of a life is measured by its sterility.
mod_sentences: As a modern writer observed, "One is not obliged to be a fool."
The ways of living I am about to examine derive their full significance only when contrasted with their opposites.
A minor clerk in a post office is the exact equal of a conqueror, provided both possess the same lucid awareness.
From this perspective, all experiences are fundamentally equal.
Certain experiences either serve a person or do them a disservice.
They serve a person only if they remain fully conscious of them.
Otherwise, the circumstance matters little: a person’s failure reflects not on external conditions, but on themselves.
I select here only individuals whose sole aim is to burn through their vitality, or who visibly expend their lives without reservation.
That choice implies nothing beyond itself.
For now, I wish to speak only of a world where thoughts, like human lives, possess no future.
Everything that drives human labor and ambition depends on the illusion of hope.
The only thought that does not lie, therefore, is a sterile thought.
Within an absurd world, the true value of an idea—or of a life—is measured precisely by its refusal to bear fruit for an imagined future.
pairs.move: The Post-Office Clerk and the Conqueror. Camus establishes the premise of Part II: social status and worldly grandeur are irrelevant illusions. Dignity depends entirely on lucid awareness. Authentic existential living demands thought and action devoid of hope—measuring life by conscious expenditure rather than future dividends.

orig_sentences: If it were sufficient to love, things would be too easy.
The more one loves, the stronger the absurd grows.
It is not through lack of love that Don Juan goes from woman to woman.
It is ridiculous to represent him as a mystic in quest of total love.
But it is indeed because he loves them with the same passion and each time with his whole self that he must repeat his gift and his profound quest.
Whence each woman hopes to give him what no one has ever given him.
Each time they are utterly wrong and merely manage to make him feel the need of that repetition.
“At last,” exclaims one of them, “I have given you love.”
Can we be surprised that Don Juan laughs at this?
“At last? No,” he says, “but once more.”
Why should it be essential to love rarely in order to love much?
mod_sentences: If loving were enough, existence would be simple.
The more intensely one loves, the sharper the friction of the absurd becomes.
It is not from an inability to love that Don Juan moves from woman to woman.
It is absurd to depict him as a frustrated mystic searching for an absolute, transcendent love.
On the contrary: it is precisely because he loves each woman with identical intensity, offering his entire being each time, that he must continually repeat this total gift and quest.
This is why each woman dreams she will finally give him what no woman before has ever provided.
Each time she is completely mistaken, merely reinforcing in him the necessity of repetition.
"At last," one of them proclaims, "I have given you true love!"
Can anyone be surprised that Don Juan laughs?
"At last? No," he answers, "only once more."
Why should one have to love rarely in order to love deeply?
pairs.move: The Ethic of Quantity over Quality in Love. Romantic idealism insists that 'true love' must be singular, exclusive, and eternal. Camus demolishes this mystical trope: Don Juan is not a tragic seeker of an impossible ideal, but an absurd hero who refuses the illusion of eternity, giving himself fully to each immediate encounter.

orig_sentences: Is Don Juan melancholy?
This is not likely.
I shall barely have recourse to the legend.
That laugh, the conquering insolence, that playfulness and love of the theater are all clear and joyous.
Every healthy creature tends to multiply himself.
So it is with Don Juan.
But, furthermore, melancholy people have two reasons for being so: they don’t know or they hope.
Don Juan knows and does not hope.
He reminds one of those artists who know their limits, never go beyond them, and in that precarious interval in which they take their spiritual stand enjoy all the wonderful ease of masters.
And that is indeed genius: the intelligence that knows its frontiers.
Up to the frontier of physical death Don Juan is ignorant of melancholy.
The moment he knows, his laugh bursts forth and makes one forgive everything.
He was melancholy at the time when he hoped.
Today, on the mouth of that woman he recognizes the bitter and comforting taste of the only knowledge.
Bitter? Barely: that necessary imperfection that makes happiness perceptible!
mod_sentences: Is Don Juan a melancholic figure?
That is highly unlikely.
We hardly need to consult romantic legends to see this.
His laughter, his triumphant audacity, his sheer delight in performance and theatricality are entirely radiant and joyful.
Every healthy, vital organism naturally seeks to multiply itself; so it is with Don Juan.
Moreover, people fall into melancholy for only two reasons: either they are ignorant of reality, or they cling to hope.
Don Juan knows reality completely, and he harbors no hope.

He resembles those accomplished artists who recognize their exact boundaries, never exceed them, and within that narrow, precarious space where they take their stand, command all the graceful mastery of genius.
And that is true genius: an intellect fully conscious of its frontiers.
Right up to the boundary of physical death, Don Juan remains untouched by melancholy.
The moment clarity dawns on him, his laughter rings out, sweeping away all reproach.
He was melancholy only back when he still clung to hope.
Today, upon the lips of the woman before him, he tastes the astringent, bracing flavor of the only knowledge that exists.
Bitter? Hardly—merely that essential imperfection that renders human happiness tangible.
pairs.move: Melancholy Belongs to Hope, Not Lucidity. Melancholy is born from two sources: ignorance of mortal limits or agonizing longing for an eternity. Don Juan eliminates both. Because he accepts his finite horizon, his joy is unpoisoned by regret. Like a master artist working strictly within the constraints of his medium, Don Juan masters living within mortality.

orig_sentences: It is quite false to try to see in Don Juan a man brought up on Ecclesiastes.
For nothing is vanity to him except the hope of another life.
He proves this because he gambles that other life against heaven itself.
Longing for desire killed by satisfaction, that commonplace of the impotent man, does not belong to him.
That is all right for Faust, who believed in God enough to sell himself to the devil.
For Don Juan the thing is simpler.
Molina’s Burlador ever replies to the threats of hell: “What a long respite you give me!”
What comes after death is futile, and what a long succession of days for whoever knows how to be alive!
Faust craved worldly goods; the poor man had only to stretch out his hand.
It already amounted to selling his soul when he was unable to gladden it.
As for satiety, Don Juan insists upon it, on the contrary.
If he leaves a woman it is not absolutely because he has ceased to desire her.
A beautiful woman is always desirable.
But he desires another, and no, this is not the same thing.
mod_sentences: It is entirely mistaken to view Don Juan as a disciple of Ecclesiastes, murmuring that all is vanity.
For him, nothing is vanity except the promise of another life.
He demonstrates this by wagering any supposed afterlife against the immediate pleasures of the earth.
The weary disillusionment that follows satisfaction—that cliché of the emotionally exhausted—is alien to him.
That weary posture suits Faust, whose belief in God was still strong enough to warrant bargaining with the Devil.
For Don Juan, the matter is far more direct.
In Tirso de Molina's play, the Trickster answers every threat of damnation with the same refrain: "What a generous respite you grant me!"
Whatever lies beyond death is irrelevant; what matters is the boundless succession of days granted to anyone who truly knows how to live.
Faust hungered for worldly mastery, yet the poor wretch had only to reach out his hand to seize it.
He had already bartered his soul away the moment he proved incapable of bringing it joy.
Don Juan, by contrast, embraces satiety fully.
When he departs from a woman, it is never simply because he has ceased to desire her.
A beautiful woman remains permanently desirable.
But he desires another woman, and those two desires are entirely distinct.
pairs.move: Don Juan vs. Faust (The Refusal of Transcendent Bargains). Faust is an intellectual who secretly believes in the absolute and trades his soul out of spiritual impotence. Don Juan has no truck with the supernatural; hell is an empty threat because eternity is meaningless. Molina's line ('What a long respite you grant me!') anchors his focus on the concrete span of life.

orig_sentences: This life gratifies his every wish, and nothing is worse than losing it.
This madman is a great wise man.
But men who live on hope do not thrive in this universe where kindness yields to generosity, affection to virile silence, and communion to solitary courage.
And all hasten to say: “He was a weakling, an idealist or a saint.”
One has to disparage the greatness that insults.
mod_sentences: This mortal life satisfies his every desire, and no catastrophe exceeds the tragedy of losing it.
What ordinary society brands a madman is, in truth, an accomplished sage.
Yet those who survive on hope cannot breathe in a world where polite sentiment yields to lavish generosity, easy affection to resolute silence, and herd solidarity to solitary courage.
Thus moralists rush to dismiss him: "He was merely an unstable weakling, an unfulfilled idealist, or a latent saint."
Mediocrity always feels compelled to demean a greatness that exposes its own cowardice.
pairs.move: The Sage Branded as Madman. Conventional morality denounces Don Juan because his radical focus on mortal enjoyment insults their self-righteous asceticism. Camus contrasts conventional herd virtues (politeness, sentimental warmth, reliance on community) with absurd virtues (magnanimity, resolute silence, solitary courage).

orig_sentences: People are sufficiently annoyed (or that smile of complicity that debases what it admires) by Don Juan’s speeches and by that same remark that he uses on all women.
But to anyone who seeks quantity in his joys, the only thing that matters is efficacy.
What is the use of complicating the passwords that have stood the test?
No one, neither the woman nor the man, listens to them, but rather to the voice that pronounces them.
They are the rule, the convention, and the courtesy.
After they are spoken the most important still remains to be done.
Don Juan is already getting ready for it.
Why should he give himself a problem in morality?
He is not like Milosz’s Mañara, who damns himself through a desire to be a saint.
Hell for him is a thing to be provoked.
He has but one reply to divine wrath, and that is human honor: “I have honor,” he says to the Commander, “and I am keeping my promise because I am a knight.”
But it would be just as great an error to make an immoralist of him.
In this regard, he is “like everyone else”: he has the moral code of his likes and dislikes.
Don Juan can be properly understood only by constant reference to what he commonly symbolizes: the ordinary seducer and the sexual athlete.
He is an ordinary seducer.
Except for the difference that he is conscious, and that is why he is absurd.
A seducer who has become lucid will not change for all that.
Seducing is his condition in life.
Only in novels does one change condition or become better.
Yet it can be said that at the same time nothing is changed and everything is transformed.
What Don Juan realizes in action is an ethic of quantity, whereas the saint, on the contrary, tends toward quality.
Not to believe in the profound meaning of things belongs to the absurd man.
As for those cordial or wonder-struck faces, he eyes them, stores them up, and does not pause over them.
Time keeps up with him.
The absurd man is he who is not apart from time.
Don Juan does not think of “collecting” women.
He exhausts their number and with them his chances of life.
“Collecting” amounts to being capable of living off one’s past.
But he rejects regret, that other form of hope.
He is incapable of looking at portraits.
mod_sentences: Critics are perpetually irritated—or wear that sly, condescending smirk that cheapens whatever it secretly envies—by Don Juan's standard declarations and the repeated lines he addresses to every woman.
Yet for anyone pursuing an ethic of quantitative joy, the only criterion is practical efficacy.
Why complicate passwords that have already proven their power?
Neither the woman nor the man truly analyzes the literal words; what moves them is the living voice that delivers them.
They serve as the opening ritual, the established convention, and the required courtesy.
Once spoken, the essential work still lies ahead, and Don Juan is already bracing for it.
Why should he invent artificial moral dilemmas for himself?
He bears no resemblance to Milosz's Miguel Mañara, who courts damnation out of an inverted hunger for sainthood.
For Don Juan, the threat of hell is something to be openly defied.
To divine wrath he offers only a single defense: human honor.
"I possess honor," he informs the Stone Commander, "and I keep my word because I am a gentleman."
Yet it would be an equal mistake to classify him as a dogmatic immoralist.
In this respect he is like everyone else: his morality consists entirely of his genuine sympathies and antipathies.
Don Juan can only be understood by returning to what he fundamentally represents: the ordinary seducer and the relentless sensualist.
He is, in essence, an ordinary seducer.
With the sole distinction that he is fully conscious, and for that exact reason, he is absurd.
A seducer who attains radical clarity will not suddenly renounce his nature.
Seduction is his vital condition.
It is only in didactic novels that human beings magically change their nature or achieve moral improvement.
Yet one can say that while nothing on the surface changes, everything is fundamentally transformed.
What Don Juan enacts through his behavior is an ethic of quantity, directly opposing the saint's pursuit of qualitative perfection.
Refusing to believe in hidden metaphysical meanings is the hallmark of the absurd person.
As for those welcoming or spellbound faces, he takes them in, absorbs them, and never lingers.
Time marches in step with him.
The absurd man is one who refuses to detach himself from time.
Don Juan does not "collect" women like souvenirs.
He exhausts their number, and in doing so, exhausts his mortal possibilities.
"Collecting" implies an ability to feed on memories of the past.
But Don Juan rejects nostalgia, which is merely hope turned backward.
He cannot bear to gaze at portraits.
pairs.move: Conscious Sensualism vs. Moral Conversion. Becoming lucid about life's absurdity does not convert someone into an ascetic; it sharpens their commitment to their authentic vocation. Camus also distinguishes the absurd man from the collector: collecting clings to the past (nostalgia as inverted hope), whereas Don Juan lives purely in the present instant without accumulating relics.

orig_sentences: Is he selfish for all that?
In his way, probably.
But here, too, it is essential to understand one another.
There are those who are made for living and those who are made for loving.
At least Don Juan would be inclined to say so.
But he would do so in a very few words such as he is capable of choosing.
For the love we are speaking of here is clothed in illusions of the eternal.
As all the specialists in passion teach us, there is no eternal love but what is thwarted.
There is scarcely any passion without struggle.
Such a love culminates only in the ultimate contradiction of death.
One must be Werther or nothing.
There, too, there are several ways of committing suicide, one of which is the total gift and forgetfulness of self.
Don Juan, as well as anyone else, knows that this can be stirring.
But he is one of the very few who know that this is not the important thing.
He knows just as well that those who turn away from all personal life through a great love enrich themselves perhaps but certainly impoverish those their love has chosen.
A mother or a passionate wife necessarily has a closed heart, for it is turned away from the world.
A single emotion, a single creature, a single face, but all is devoured.
Quite a different love disturbs Don Juan, and this one is liberating.
It brings with it all the faces in the world, and its tremor comes from the fact that it knows itself to be mortal.
Don Juan has chosen to be nothing.
mod_sentences: Does this make him fundamentally selfish?
In his own way, perhaps.
Yet here, too, we must define our terms carefully.
There are those born for living, and those born for loving—or so Don Juan would argue, using the spare, precise vocabulary natural to him.
At least Don Juan would be inclined to frame it in those terms.
And he would express it in the few sharp words he chooses with such precision.
For romantic love, as traditionally conceived, cloaks itself in fantasies of eternity.
As every chronicler of tragic romance demonstrates, the only love that feels eternal is a thwarted love.
Passion rarely thrives without obstacles and agony.
Such romantic adoration inevitably culminates in the ultimate contradiction: death.
One must either become Werther or remain nothing.
In romance, too, there are numerous forms of suicide, not least of which is the total surrender and dissolution of self in another.
Don Juan understands as well as anyone that such self-immolation can be emotionally moving.
Yet he is among the rare few who realize that it is fundamentally beside the point.

He recognizes that those who abandon their own independent life for the sake of a grand passion may enrich their own emotional drama, but they inevitably drain and suffocate the person they claim to adore.
A possessive mother or an obsessively devoted wife inevitably possesses a constricted heart, because it has closed itself off from the wider world.
A single emotion, a single person, a single face—and everything else is consumed.
Don Juan is stirred by a completely different love: an expansive, liberating passion.
It embraces every face under the sun, and its exquisite tremor arises from the lucid awareness that it is finite and mortal.
Don Juan has consciously chosen to surrender any claim to permanent identity.
pairs.move: Romantic Monogamy as Covert Suicide vs. Generous Ephemeral Love. Camus exposes the romantic cult of 'grand passion' (Werther) as a death drive: romantic obsession demands impossible eternity and ends in mutual suffocation or literal suicide. Don Juan's love is expansive and non-possessive; acknowledging its mortality, it leaves the beloved free and rejoices in the living world.

orig_sentences: For him it is a matter of seeing clearly.
We call love what binds us to certain creatures only by reference to a collective way of seeing for which books and legends are responsible.
But of love I know only that mixture of desire, affection, and intelligence that binds me to this or that creature.
That compound is not the same for another person.
I do not have the right to cover all these experiences with the same name.
This exempts one from conducting them with the same gestures.
The absurd man multiplies here again what he cannot unify.
Thus he discovers a new way of being which liberates him at least as much as it liberates those who approach him.
There is no noble love but that which recognizes itself to be both short-lived and exceptional.
All those deaths and all those rebirths gathered together as in a sheaf make up for Don Juan the flowering of his life.
It is his way of giving and of vivifying.
I let it be decided whether or not one can speak of selfishness.
mod_sentences: For him, everything reduces to seeing clearly.
We assign the word "love" to the bond tying us to particular individuals only by relying on cultural myths manufactured by novels and folklore.
In reality, all I directly experience of love is that unique fusion of desire, tenderness, and intellectual affinity binding me to a specific human being.
That exact combination cannot be duplicated with anyone else.
I have no right to paste the same generic label over radically diverse encounters.
Refusing to use a single label frees one from approaching each person with identical, scripted gestures.
Here again, the absurd man multiplies what he is powerless to unify.
In doing so, he discovers a mode of existence that liberates him every bit as much as it frees those who enter his life.
There is no truly noble love other than that which understands itself to be simultaneously transient and rare.
All those successive endings and rebirths, bound together like a rich harvest, constitute for Don Juan the full flowering of his existence.
This is his unique way of giving of himself and breathing vitality into others.
I leave it to the reader to decide whether this can legitimately be called selfishness.
pairs.move: Demystifying Romantic Vocabulary. The universal concept of 'Love' is an abstraction borrowed from literature. Real emotional experience is always particular, transient, and unrepeatable. The absurd strategy is to multiply concrete encounters rather than attempting to force them into a single, unified metaphysical category.

orig_sentences: I think at this point of all those who absolutely insist that Don Juan be punished.
Not only in another life, but even in this one.
I think of all those tales, legends, and laughs about the aged Don Juan.
But Don Juan is already ready.
To a conscious man old age and what it portends are not a surprise.
Indeed, he is conscious only in so far as he does not conceal its horror from himself.
There was in Athens a temple dedicated to old age.
Children were taken there.
As for Don Juan, the more people laugh at him, the more his figure stands out.
Thereby he rejects the one the romantics lent him.
No one wants to laugh at that tormented, pitiful Don Juan.
He is pitied; heaven itself will redeem him?
But that’s not it.
In the universe of which Don Juan has a glimpse, ridicule too is included.
He would consider it normal to be chastised.
That is the rule of the game.
And, indeed, it is typical of his nobility to have accepted all the rules of the game.
Yet he knows he is right and that there can be no question of punishment.
A fate is not a punishment.
mod_sentences: At this point, I think of all those moralists who demand that Don Juan be punished—not merely in the next world, but within this one.
They insist he must suffer retribution not only in eternity, but in his earthly life.
I think of the endless cautionary tales, folklore, and derisive mockery directed at the aging Don Juan.
But Don Juan is already prepared.
To a lucid human being, physical aging and everything it entails come as no surprise.
Indeed, one is truly conscious only to the extent that one refuses to hide from the grim reality of decay.
In ancient Athens, there stood a temple dedicated to Old Age.
Children were taken there to behold their future.
As for Don Juan, the louder society laughs at his physical decline, the more majestic his stature becomes.
By accepting this ridicule, he shatters the romantic caricature of himself.
No one wants to laugh at the brooding, pitiful Don Juan invented by the Romantics.
Instead, people pity him and imagine that heaven will eventually redeem him.
But that is a sentimental distortion.
Within the absurd cosmos Don Juan perceives, mockery is part of the landscape.
He regards social condemnation as perfectly natural.
That is simply part of the rules of the game.
And it is the hallmark of his aristocratic nobility to have accepted every rule of the game without complaint.
Yet in his core, he knows he is justified, and that talk of moral retribution is meaningless.
A mortal destiny is not a divine punishment.
pairs.move: Destiny vs. Punishment (Aging and Ridicule). Society demands that the aging seducer suffer humiliation as divine retribution for his sensuality. Camus counters that biological decay is not moral punishment, but the universal human fate. The absurd man accepts physical degradation with open eyes, without seeking sentimental pity or religious redemption.

orig_sentences: That is his crime, and how easy it is to understand why the men of God call down punishment on his head.
He achieves a knowledge without illusions which negates everything they profess.
Loving and possessing, conquering and consuming—that is his way of knowing.
(There is significance in that favorite Scriptural word that calls the carnal act “knowing.”)
He is their worst enemy to the extent that he is ignorant of them.
A chronicler relates that the true Burlador died assassinated by Franciscans who wanted “to put an end to the excesses and blasphemies of Don Juan, whose birth assured him impunity.”
Then they proclaimed that heaven had struck him down.
No one has proved that strange end.
Nor has anyone proved the contrary.
But without wondering if it is probable, I can say that it is logical.
I want merely to single out at this point the word “birth” and to play on words: it was the fact of living that assured his innocence.
It was from death alone that he derived a guilt now become legendary.
mod_sentences: That is his true transgression, and it is easy to see why religious authorities demand vengeance upon his head.
He achieves an uncompromising clarity that invalidates everything they preach.
Loving and possessing, conquering and expending—this is his method of knowing the world.
(It is deeply revealing that the biblical idiom refers to the carnal act itself as "knowing.")
He is their most dangerous adversary precisely because he pays them no mind.

An ancient chronicler records that the historical Trickster of Seville was assassinated in secret by Franciscan monks who wished "to terminate the outrages and blasphemies of a Don Juan whose noble birth guaranteed him impunity."
The friars then publicly announced that divine wrath had struck him dead.
No historian has verified that bizarre account.
Nor has anyone managed to refute it.
Yet without debating its historical probability, one can affirm its poetic logic.
I wish only to focus here on the word "birth" and make a deliberate play upon it: it was the raw fact of being alive that established his innocence.
It was solely from death that moralists manufactured the legendary guilt attached to his name.
pairs.move: Carnal Knowledge as Epistemological Heresy. By grounding knowledge purely in physical experience ('knowing' in the Biblical sense), Don Juan invalidates religious claims to transcendent authority. The church had to invent divine retribution (or murder him and blame God) because an unpunished, joyful mortal exposes religious guilt as an artificial construct.

orig_sentences: What else does that stone Commander signify, that cold statue set in motion to punish the blood and courage that dared to think?
All the powers of eternal Reason, of order, of universal morality, all the foreign grandeur of a God open to wrath are summed up in him.
That gigantic and soulless stone merely symbolizes the forces that Don Juan negated forever.
But the Commander’s mission stops there.
The thunder and lightning can return to the imitation heaven whence they were called forth.
The real tragedy takes place quite apart from them.
No, it was not under a stone hand that Don Juan met his death.
I am inclined to believe in the legendary bravado, in that mad laughter of the healthy man provoking a non-existent God.

But, above all, I believe that on that evening when Don Juan was waiting at Anna’s the Commander didn’t come, and that after midnight the blasphemer must have felt the dreadful bitterness of those who have been right.
I accept even more readily the account of his life that has him eventually burying himself in a monastery.
Not that the edifying aspect of the story can be considered probable.
What refuge can he go ask of God?
But this symbolizes rather the logical outcome of a life completely imbued with the absurd, the grim ending of an existence turned toward short-lived joys.
At this point sensual pleasure winds up in asceticism.
It is essential to realize that they may be, as it were, the two aspects of the same destitution.

What more ghastly image can be called up than that of a man betrayed by his body who, simply because he did not die in time, lives out the comedy while awaiting the end, face to face with that God he does not adore, serving him as he served life, kneeling before a void and arms outstretched toward a heaven without eloquence that he knows to be also without depth?
mod_sentences: What else does the Stone Commander embody—that frozen statue brought to life to crush the living pulse of a man who dared to think for himself?
In that statue are concentrated all the dictates of cosmic Reason, institutional order, universal morality, and the alien majesty of an angry God.
That colossal, lifeless monument of stone merely personifies the external dogmas Don Juan rejected his entire life.
Yet the Commander's dramatic role ends right there.
The theatrical thunder and lightning can return to the artificial stage ceiling from which they were summoned.
The genuine tragedy unfolds entirely elsewhere.
No, Don Juan did not meet his end crushed beneath a stone handshake.
I am certainly ready to believe in the legendary defiance—in the wild, defiant laughter of a vital man challenging a non-existent deity.

But above all, I believe that on the evening Don Juan waited for his final reckoning, the Stone Commander never showed up at all—and that past midnight, the blasphemer experienced the crushing, bitter desolation of those who have been entirely correct all along.
I find it even easier to accept the historical tradition in which Don Juan ends his days secluded inside a monastery.
Not that the pious moral of the story holds any water: what possible sanctuary could he ask from a God he does not believe in?
What refuge could he conceivably seek from a deity he has always denied?
Rather, this cloister represents the ultimate logical denouement of an existence steeped in the absurd—the austere finale of a life devoted exclusively to fleeting pleasures.
At this threshold, extreme sensuality folds into extreme asceticism.
One must understand that these two extremes are merely opposite faces of the identical existential poverty.

What more haunting spectacle could one imagine than a man betrayed by his aging flesh, who—simply because he failed to die in the prime of life—plays out the theatrical farce to the very end: confronting a God he does not worship, performing religious rituals with the same mechanical detachment with which he once pursued seduction, kneeling before an absolute void, with arms outstretched toward a silent heaven he knows to be utterly devoid of depth?
pairs.move: The Stone Commander Never Came: The Desolation of Being Right. The greatest existential insight in the essay: the terrifying realization is not that God punishes the rebel, but that God never appears. Seduction and monastic asceticism are two sides of the same coin: living fully within physical reality without transcendent illusions. Don Juan kneeling in an empty chapel before a silent void is the ultimate absurd hero.

orig_sentences: I see Don Juan in a cell of one of those Spanish monasteries lost on a hilltop.

And if he contemplates anything at all, it is not the ghosts of past loves, but perhaps, through a narrow slit in the sun-baked wall, some silent Spanish plain, a noble, soulless land in which he recognizes himself.
Yes, it is on this melancholy and radiant image that the curtain must be rung down.
The ultimate end, awaited but never desired, the ultimate end is negligible.
mod_sentences: I envision Don Juan in the cell of an isolated Spanish monastery perched high upon an arid hilltop.

And if he gazes out at anything at all, it is certainly not the phantom memories of forgotten lovers, but rather—framed through a narrow slit in the sun-baked stone wall—the silent, sweeping Spanish plateau: an austere, soulless expanse in which he recognizes his own nature.
Yes, it is upon this melancholic yet luminous tableau that the theatrical curtain must descend.
That final death—inevitable, never sought, yet completely anticipated—remains fundamentally negligible.
pairs.move: The Arid Landscape of Radical Lucidity. In the final scene, Don Juan achieves perfect harmony with the absurd: looking out over the barren, sun-drenched Spanish plateau—a landscape as indifferent, austere, and soulless as his own lucid mind. Death is neither feared nor courted; it is merely an indifferent terminus to a fully expended life.
